title: When the Pritzkers went to Shibuya
tagline: How the Nippon Foundation talked sixteen architects into rebuilding a Tokyo ward's most overlooked civic buildings — the public toilets.
intro: For most of the postwar period, the public toilets scattered through Shibuya were governed by what the Japanese call the four Ks — kusai, kurai, kowai, kitanai: smelly, dark, scary, dirty. People avoided them, especially at night, especially women, especially anyone with a stroller or a wheelchair. In 2018 the Nippon Foundation, a private philanthropic body, decided to fix this by going a very long way around. It commissioned sixteen architects and designers — a roster heavy with Pritzker Prize laureates — to rebuild seventeen toilets across the ward, and asked the photographer Satoshi Nagare to document every one of them in a single unified visual record. The first pair opened in August 2020. By 2023 the project had its own film, made by Wim Wenders, and a small but determined tourist circuit had formed in Shibuya. This is the story of how that happened, and what the buildings actually do.

sections.heading: The architecture
sections.body:
The most famous of the seventeen sits in Yoyogi Fukamachi Mini Park. Shigeru Ban — already a Pritzker laureate when he took the brief — addressed the fears people have about using a public restroom by the most direct means available: he made the walls see-through. From the outside, anyone can confirm at a glance that the stall is clean and unoccupied. Lock the door, and the smart glass flips opaque. A near-identical sibling sits ten minutes' walk away in Haru-no-Ogawa Community Park, three coloured cubes arranged as a small constellation in the park, each lit at night in a different hue. Together they were the toilets that went viral worldwide and gave the project its early oxygen.

Elsewhere in the ward the architecture turns inward. Tadao Ando's Amayadori at Jingu-Dori Park is a five-square-metre concrete drum wrapped in vertical louvres, with an engawa walkway tucked beneath the eaves. "I sought for this small architecture to exceed the boundaries of a public toilet," Ando wrote, "to become a place in the urban landscape." Toyo Ito split his contribution into three rounded white mushrooms beside the Yoyogi-Hachiman shrine. Kengo Kuma broke his into five cedar-clad huts strung along a path through Nabeshima Shoto Park — a village in miniature. And at Ebisu East Park, Fumihiko Maki slid a thin white roof above three small volumes around an open courtyard; locals, eyeing the slide nearby, nicknamed it the Squid.

sections.heading: The non-architects
sections.body:
What sets the Tokyo Toilet apart from a normal architectural commission is who else got asked. The Foundation deliberately reached past the architectural shortlist. Marc Newson, the Australian industrial designer better known for chairs, Apple Watches and aircraft interiors, made what is among his only completed works of public architecture: a mint-green hut on a quiet Urasando side street, modelled on a Japanese teahouse and finished with an untreated copper roof that will weather into a soft patina over decades. NIGO — Tomoaki Nagao, the founder of A Bathing Ape and now creative director of Kenzo — drew on neighbourhood history instead, building a small red-roofed American cottage at Jingumae as a Pop-art nod to the postwar Washington Heights military housing that once stood on the site.

Nao Tamura, a New York-based product designer, was handed the trickiest plot — a thin triangle wedged between a residential street and a railway — and answered with three vermilion volumes whose folded eaves quote Origata, the Japanese art of decorative gift-wrapping. The three stalls are unisex and fully independent, designed, drawing on her years in New York's LGBTQ+ community, so that no one has to gender themselves at the door. Kashiwa Sato, the graphic designer behind Uniqlo's global identity, produced the project's quietest gesture: a pure-white louvered box at Ebisu Station's west exit, plus the rounded, friendly pictogram system that runs across all seventeen sites. Masamichi Katayama of Wonderwall, a retail-interior specialist, scattered fifteen randomly rotated concrete walls through a small Ebisu park and called the result Modern Kawaya — a reference to the semi-public squat-shelters Japanese villagers improvised long before plumbing arrived. Takenosuke Sakakura's Andon at Nishihara Itchome rounds out the set: a mint-tinted lantern whose frosted glass is etched with a tree-branch pattern, conjuring greenery in a park that has almost none. (Sou Fujimoto's Toilet in Nature, often lumped in with the project, is in fact a separate commission, in Chiba prefecture — worth the trip, but a different story.)

sections.heading: After the build
sections.body:
Then came the cleaner. In 2023 Wim Wenders released Perfect Days, a film built around a fictional maintenance worker who washes the Tokyo Toilets in unhurried, ritualistic detail. It won Kōji Yakusho the Best Actor prize at Cannes and ran the festival circuit for a year — by far the strangest publicity vehicle a public works project has ever enjoyed. Press followed: Dezeen, Wallpaper, the New York Times, Monocle. A walking tour formed itself organically through Shibuya, Yoyogi and Ebisu. The toilets did the thing they had been asked to do; the four Ks receded.

The less-told half of the story is operational. None of this would have held up without the maintenance regime that Shibuya City worked out with TOTO and a dedicated cleaning crew — three sweeps a day, in some cases more, on a coordinated schedule that survived the launch hype. Design alone never made a public toilet pleasant; design plus a cleaning rota did. The result is the loop the project quietly bet on: better toilets attract more public use, more public use creates more reason to maintain them well, and a row of small Pritzker-grade buildings keeps doing the unglamorous work of being open at three in the morning, lit, and clean.

title: The world's most serious roadside loos
tagline: How Norway turned the public toilet into a national landscape-architecture program — and convinced foreigners to drive 2,000 kilometres to use one.
intro: In 1994, the Norwegian Public Roads Administration — Statens vegvesen, the agency that paves the roads and plows the snow — quietly began commissioning architects to design its rest stops. Not signage. Not picnic tables. The toilets. Three decades on, the Nasjonale turistveger program covers eighteen designated 'scenic routes' running from the Lofoten Islands to the Hardangerfjord, and the brief is unchanged: a leading Norwegian or Scandinavian studio gets a tiny budget, a vast view, and instructions to design something that belongs to the landscape. Snøhetta, Reiulf Ramstad, Code Arkitektur, Haugen/Zohar, Morfeus — all of them have built public restrooms here. A small bench of house photographers — Roger Ellingsen, Steinar Skaar, Jarle Wæhler, Frid-Jorunn Stabell, Werner Harstad — quietly documents each one in a unified visual language. The result is the most architecturally serious roadside-bathroom program on earth, and a long argument that civic infrastructure can be made with the same care as a concert hall.

sections.heading: The commissions
sections.body:
The roster reads like a Nordic architecture syllabus. At Eggum, on the Lofoten Scenic Route, Snøhetta — yes, that Snøhetta, of the Oslo Opera House and the September 11 Memorial Pavilion — delivered what is reportedly the firm's smallest completed building: a curved gabion amphitheatre that dishes a kiosk and toilet straight into a stone wall. The gabion language was lifted from Borga, a German WWII radar ruin sharing the same hilltop, and the building terminates a paved path running from concrete bunker to open sea. At Ureddplassen, 700 kilometres north on the Helgelandskysten coast, Haugen/Zohar Arkitekter set a swooping marble bench and a frosted-glass toilet on a polished travertine platform — the site is a memorial to HNoMS Uredd, a Norwegian submarine lost in 1943, and the WC's interior light is calibrated low enough not to drown out the aurora.

Further north still, at Selvika on the Havøysund route above the 70th parallel, Reiulf Ramstad Arkitekter designed a rest area that is mostly a journey: a zig-zag of board-formed concrete walls slows visitors down through a Barents-facing bay. At the bottom, lodged inside the sweeping ribbon, sits the toilet itself — a small concrete chamber punched with three circular portholes of different sizes. The architecture turns a bathroom break into a choreographed descent.

sections.heading: Disappearing acts
sections.body:
The Scenic Routes brief is, in essence, a very strange one. A designer is handed a tiny program — one accessible WC, sometimes a shelter, occasionally a kiosk — and asked to engage a landscape that would humiliate most buildings. The Norwegian solution, repeated across the program, is to make the toilet disappear into something more important. At Bukkekjerka on the island of Andøya, Morfeus Arkitekter (Caroline Støvring and Cecilie Wille, with Margrethe Rosenlund and Mari Høstmælingen Grennæs) clad a small cubicle in one-way mirrored glass beside a rock formation long held sacred by the local Sámi. From outside, the toilet vanishes into a reflection of lichen-orange stone; from inside, the user looks out through what becomes, in the architects' words, a private cinema of the Norwegian Sea.

At Utsikten on the Gaularfjellet route, Code Arkitektur went further: the building IS the platform. An 80-centimetre-thin triangular concrete deck cantilevers out over a fjord valley, its three corners flared upward like origami folds. One corner houses seating, one frames terrain access, and the third — a slim rectangular slot carved into the concrete — opens to a solar-powered toilet. The visitor barely registers the program. Norway's Scenic Routes have, over thirty years, hardened this into a national convention: the bathroom should be a hinge, not a hero. The view does the work.

sections.heading: A long game
sections.body:
The program is currently scheduled to run until 2029. Other countries have tried similar interventions — Iceland's Ring Road has experimented with designer rest stops; the UK has funded a handful of architectural loos — but nothing approaches the Norwegian scale, longevity, or photographic discipline. The visitor economics have shifted accordingly: architecture-tour operators now sell itineraries built around the routes, and a non-trivial share of foreign drivers on the Helgelandskysten or Andøya are, by their own admission, there for the buildings.

There is a quieter cultural dividend, too. Snøhetta's later international ascent — the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, Times Square's reconstruction, Le Monde's Paris headquarters — traces partly back to early Scenic Routes commissions like Eggum, where a young Oslo studio got to build for a real client, on a real coastline, with the latitude to refuse a generic answer. Reiulf Ramstad, Code, Haugen/Zohar, Morfeus all benefited from the same patient training ground. The toilet, it turns out, is not a punchline. It is a country's way of teaching itself how to build.

title: When the toilet is the destination
tagline: Five public toilets that visitors do not stumble upon — they travel for them, queue for them, and occasionally steal them.
intro: A public toilet is, almost by definition, infrastructure that happens to be at a destination. You came for the museum, the temple, the trailhead, the mall; the toilet is the thing that makes staying possible. This story is about the inversion. In a 1,500-person town in Northland, in a 600-year-old Kyoto monastery, in a Nanjing shopping centre, on a campus in southwest Delhi, and for one strange year on the fifth floor of the Guggenheim, the toilet itself is the visit. People plan around it, queue for it, photograph it, write about it. What links these five cases is the visitor's primary reason for being there. What distinguishes them is the mechanism: civic identity, historic preservation, retail spectacle, sanitation advocacy, and contemporary art. Five different routes to the same unlikely endpoint — a toilet that pulls people in.

sections.heading: Markers of place
sections.body:
The Hundertwasser Toilets in Kawakawa and the Tōsu at Tōfuku-ji sit at opposite ends of architectural history and yet do the same civic work: they tell visitors that they have arrived. Kawakawa is a Northland rail-stop town of roughly 1,500 people. In 1997 its business association approached Friedensreich Hundertwasser — the Austrian artist-architect who had made New Zealand his second home — to redesign a 1960s concrete-block public loo on the main road. He personally supervised every detail until his death in 2000, making it his last completed work: wavy roofline, mosaics laid by Bay of Islands College students, recycled bottles embedded as windows, a living plane tree on the roof. The town now draws around 250,000 visitors a year for it; in 2020 Te Hononga Hundertwasser Memorial Park opened next door, and in 2023 Heritage New Zealand listed the toilet as a Category 1 historic place, alongside Christchurch Cathedral.

Tōfuku-ji's Tōsu, built around 1425 for the monastery's resident monks, predates Kawakawa's by nearly six centuries and asks nothing of you. It is a long wooden hall of evenly-spaced pit holes in an earthen floor — the so-called hyakusecchin, the 'hundred-person toilet,' used in strict ritual silence as part of Zen practice. No one uses it any more. Visitors look in through a wooden lattice from outside. It is designated an Important Cultural Property of Japan because the temple kept it, instead of replacing it, and now it serves as evidence that even in the 15th century, sanitation could be a building worth saving.

sections.heading: The teaching toilets
sections.body:
The Sulabh International Museum of Toilets in Delhi and the themed washrooms at Deji Plaza in Nanjing have almost nothing in common ideologically — and yet both are organised on the same proposition, which is that a toilet can be the primary attraction if you stage it as one. Sulabh was founded in 1992 by the late Dr Bindeshwar Pathak, a sanitation reformer whose larger NGO has spent half a century propagating dry twin-pit ecosan technology across India, work that earned him the Padma Bhushan and the Stockholm Water Prize. The museum on Sulabh's southwest Delhi campus is a fully curated history of the toilet from 2500 BCE to the present, arranged across Ancient, Medieval and Modern wings — Roman latrine replicas, illustrated chamber pots, Japanese washlets, a gilded model of Louis XIV's commode-throne, an antique 1145 CE privy. The didactic intent is unmissable: the toilet here is a teaching artifact about caste, hygiene, and global development.

Deji Plaza, in central Nanjing, is the same logic in commercial reverse. Since 2021 the mall has commissioned the Shanghai studio X+Living, led by Li Xiang, to design a different themed washroom on every floor — the 2022 sixth-floor 'Sanctuary Garden' with its botanical lattices, green marble fountain-basins and petal-shaped sofas; a 2023 houndstooth-clad 'Blues Club' on the second floor; reportedly a sapphire-blue 'Palace' and a cyberpunk room costing tens of millions of yuan. Chinese press treats the program as a scenic attraction; the mall openly reports that around 30 percent of foot traffic is restroom-driven, with roughly 40 percent of those visitors converting into purchases. A museum and a mall, both with their toilets in the window.

sections.heading: Three minutes, gold-plated
sections.body:
Of the five, Maurizio Cattelan's America (2016) is the only one where the destination is not the building, or the collection, or the brand, but the experience itself. The Italian artist installed an 18-karat solid-gold working toilet in a small public bathroom on the Guggenheim's fifth floor and let anyone with a museum ticket queue up and use it. Over its year-long run, roughly 100,000 people did. The work was billed as 'one percent art for the ninety-nine percent,' a wry commentary on luxury and American excess; in practice it was a line, a guard, a closed door, three minutes alone with a gold seat. In 2019 it travelled to Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire for a special exhibition and, five days after opening, was stolen at five in the morning. It has never been recovered.

What the five share, in the end, is that the verb of the visit changes. You do not visit Kawakawa and then use the toilet; you visit the toilet, and Kawakawa is what happens around it. At Deji Plaza, the washroom is the storefront. At Sulabh, the chamber pot is the lesson. At the Guggenheim, briefly, the bathroom was the gallery. Using the toilet stops being a byproduct of the trip. It becomes the trip.
